learningObjectives.title: Five kinds of formula and how to interconvert them
The functional groups and the classes they define
Why boiling points rise along a series
Structural isomers, and primary, secondary, tertiary
¹H NMR: environments, chemical shift and integration
Splitting patterns and the n + 1 rule

questions.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formula of a hydrocarbon. Which condensed structural formula represents the same compound?
options: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃
CH₃CH₂(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
optionWhy: You counted the six line segments as six carbon atoms. The lines are bonds; the carbon atoms sit at the line ends and vertices, so the main chain has six carbons, not five, and the branch adds a seventh.

You gave the second carbon two H atoms as if it were an ordinary chain carbon. It is bonded to three carbon atoms, so it can carry only one H atom; written as CH₂ with a CH₃ attached it would have five bonds.

You counted every line end and vertex as a carbon atom: six in the main chain and one at the end of the branch on the second carbon. That carbon is bonded to three carbon atoms, so it is CH; the rest are CH₃ at the ends and CH₂ in the chain. The compound is 2-methylhexane, C₇H₁₆.
You ignored the short vertical line. Its end is a carbon atom too, so it is a CH₃ branch on the second carbon, and that carbon is CH, not CH₂. The compound has seven carbon atoms, not six.
questions.explain: You counted every line end and vertex as a carbon atom: six in the main chain and one at the end of the branch on the second carbon. That carbon is bonded to three carbon atoms, so it is CH; the rest are CH₃ at the ends and CH₂ in the chain. The compound is 2-methylhexane, C₇H₁₆.

questions.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formula of a compound. Which statement about its functional groups is correct?
options: It contains an amido group, since –NH₂ is bonded to a carbon atom.
It contains an ester group, since the C=O carbon is bonded to two carbons.
It is unsaturated, since an –NH₂ group has replaced a hydrogen atom.
It contains amino and ketone groups, since –NH₂ and C=O are on different carbons.
optionWhy: An amido group is –CONH₂, with the nitrogen bonded directly to the carbonyl carbon. Here the NH₂ is on a CH₂ carbon two bonds away from the C=O, so it is an amino group.
An ester group is –COO–, with the carbonyl carbon bonded to a second oxygen atom. A C=O carbon bonded to two carbon atoms is a ketone carbonyl group.
Saturated and unsaturated refer to carbon–carbon bonds. All the carbon–carbon bonds here are single, so the compound is saturated whatever functional groups it carries.

The –NH₂ group bonded to a carbon of the chain is an amino group. The C=O carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms, so it is a ketone carbonyl group. The two groups are on different carbon atoms, so there is no amide.
questions.explain: The –NH₂ group bonded to a carbon of the chain is an amino group. The C=O carbon is bonded to two carbon atoms, so it is a ketone carbonyl group. The two groups are on different carbon atoms, so there is no amide.

questions.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formulas of four compounds, P, Q, R and S. Which two are successive members of the same homologous series?
options: P and Q
Q and R
R and S
P and R
optionWhy: Their molecular formulas, C₃H₆O and C₄H₈O, differ by CH₂, but P has an aldehyde group (C=O at the end of the chain) and Q a ketone group (C=O inside the chain). Members of one series share the same functional group.
Butanone (Q) and butanal (R) have the same molecular formula, C₄H₈O, with different functional groups: they are functional group isomers, not members of one series.

Butanal (R, C₄H₈O) and butan-1-ol (S, C₄H₁₀O) have the same number of carbon atoms and differ by H₂; they belong to different series (aldehydes and alcohols). Successive members differ by CH₂ and share a functional group.
P is propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, and R is butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO: both have the aldehyde group –CHO and their formulas differ by one CH₂ unit, so they are successive aldehydes.
questions.explain: P is propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, and R is butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO: both have the aldehyde group –CHO and their formulas differ by one CH₂ unit, so they are successive aldehydes.

questions.q: The boiling points of the first five straight-chain alkanes are: methane −162 °C, ethane −89 °C, propane −42 °C, butane −1 °C and pentane 36 °C. Which statement about this trend is correct?
options: Each further CH₂ unit adds the same rise as the last, 37 °C, so hexane is expected to boil at 73 °C.
The rise is caused by hydrogen bonding, which grows as H atoms are added to the chain.
The rise per CH₂ unit shrinks along the series, so hexane is expected to boil below 73 °C.
The rise occurs because longer molecules have more C–C and C–H bonds to break.
optionWhy: The steps in the data are 73, 47, 41 and 37 °C, not a constant: each extra CH₂ unit makes a smaller proportional difference to the London forces, so the next rise is less than 37 °C.
Alkanes have no O–H or N–H bonds and form no hydrogen bonds. The only forces between alkane molecules are London forces, which strengthen as the number of electrons increases.

The steps are 73, 47, 41 and 37 °C: each added CH₂ unit strengthens the London forces by a smaller fraction of an already larger molecule, so the next step is smaller than 37 °C and hexane boils below 73 °C (it boils at 69 °C).
Boiling separates molecules from one another; no covalent bonds are broken. The trend is due to stronger London forces between longer molecules with more electrons.
questions.explain: The steps are 73, 47, 41 and 37 °C: each added CH₂ unit strengthens the London forces by a smaller fraction of an already larger molecule, so the next step is smaller than 37 °C and hexane boils below 73 °C (it boils at 69 °C).
questions.working: Successive differences: −89 − (−162) = 73 °C; −42 − (−89) = 47 °C; −1 − (−42) = 41 °C; 36 − (−1) = 37 °C. The steps decrease, so the next step is smaller than 37 °C and hexane is expected to boil below 36 + 37 = 73 °C (it boils at 69 °C).

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂OH?
options: but-1-en-4-ol
but-3-en-1-ol
but-4-en-1-ol
but-3-en-1-al
optionWhy: A student who gives the C=C bond the lowest number picks this. The group named as the suffix (-ol) has priority for the lowest locant; the double bond is numbered after it.
The chain has four carbon atoms. The –OH group, named by the suffix -ol, takes the lowest locant, 1. The C=C bond is then between carbons 3 and 4 and takes the lower number, 3: but-3-en-1-ol.
The –OH locant is right, but a C=C bond between carbons 3 and 4 takes the lower number, 3.
The suffix -al denotes an aldehyde (–CHO). This compound has a hydroxyl group, –OH, which takes the suffix -ol.
questions.explain: The chain has four carbon atoms. The –OH group, named by the suffix -ol, takes the lowest locant, 1. The C=C bond is then between carbons 3 and 4 and takes the lower number, 3: but-3-en-1-ol.

questions.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formula of a halogenoalkane. What is its IUPAC name?
options: 3-methyl-2-bromohexane
2-bromo-3-methylhexane
2-bromo-3-propylbutane
5-bromo-4-methylhexane
optionWhy: Halogen and alkyl prefixes are listed together in alphabetical order, so bromo comes before methyl, whatever the locants: 2-bromo-3-methylhexane.

Carbon atoms sit at every end and vertex: the longest chain has six, so the parent is hexane. Numbering from the right-hand end gives the substituents the lowest locants, 2 and 3 (rather than 4 and 5 from the left). Prefixes are listed alphabetically: bromo before methyl.
The parent chain is the longest continuous chain, which runs through the propyl group: six carbon atoms. A four-carbon chain with a propyl branch is not the longest choice.

The chain is numbered from the end that gives the substituents the lowest locants, not from the left-hand end of the drawing. Numbering from the right gives 2 and 3, lower than 4 and 5, so the name is 2-bromo-3-methylhexane.
questions.explain: Carbon atoms sit at every end and vertex: the longest chain has six, so the parent is hexane. Numbering from the right-hand end gives the substituents the lowest locants, 2 and 3 (rather than 4 and 5 from the left). Prefixes are listed alphabetically: bromo before methyl.
questions.working: Longest continuous chain: six carbon atoms, so the parent is hexane. Numbering from the right-hand end puts Br on C2 and CH₃ on C3 (locants 2,3); from the left they would be 5,4. Prefixes in alphabetical order: bromo before methyl. Name: 2-bromo-3-methylhexane.

questions.q: The diagram shows the skeletal formula of a compound. What is its IUPAC name?
options: 2-methylpent-2-en-4-ol
4-methylpent-4-en-2-ol
4-methylpent-3-en-2-ol
4-methylpent-3-en-2-al
optionWhy: The functional group named by the suffix (-ol) takes priority for the lowest locant, so numbering starts from the OH end: 2-ol, 3-ene and 4-methyl.
A double bond is given the lower of the numbers of its two carbon atoms. Numbered from the OH end, the C=C joins carbons 3 and 4, so it is 3-ene; the methyl group is on carbon 4.

The hydroxyl group takes the suffix -ol and the lowest locant, so numbering starts at the right-hand end: OH on carbon 2, the C=C between carbons 3 and 4, named by its lower number, 3, and the methyl group on carbon 4.
The suffix -al denotes an aldehyde, –CHO. This compound has a hydroxyl group, –OH, on carbon 2, so the suffix is -ol: 4-methylpent-3-en-2-ol.
questions.explain: The hydroxyl group takes the suffix -ol and the lowest locant, so numbering starts at the right-hand end: OH on carbon 2, the C=C between carbons 3 and 4, named by its lower number, 3, and the methyl group on carbon 4.
questions.working: The suffix -ol takes the lowest locant, so number from the right-hand end: OH on C2, C=C between C3 and C4 (locant 3), methyl on C4. Name: 4-methylpent-3-en-2-ol.

questions.q: Which compound is a structural isomer of butan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH?
options: CH₃CH₂OCH₂CH₃
CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO
HOCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃
CH₃(CH₂)₄OH
optionWhy: Ethoxyethane is C₄H₁₀O, the same molecular formula as butan-1-ol, but its atoms are connected differently (an alkoxy group instead of a hydroxyl group). It is a functional group isomer.
Butanal has four carbons and one oxygen, but its formula is C₄H₈O, two H atoms fewer than butan-1-ol (C₄H₁₀O). Isomers must have the same molecular formula.
This is butan-1-ol written from the other end. The atoms are connected in the same order, so it is the same compound, not an isomer.
Pentan-1-ol is C₅H₁₂O, one CH₂ more than butan-1-ol. It is the next member of the same homologous series, not an isomer.
questions.explain: Ethoxyethane is C₄H₁₀O, the same molecular formula as butan-1-ol, but its atoms are connected differently (an alkoxy group instead of a hydroxyl group). It is a functional group isomer.

questions.q: Which compound is a secondary halogenoalkane?
options: (CH₃)₂CBrCH₂CH₃
CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₂CH₃
CH₃CH₂CH₂CHBr₂
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂Br
optionWhy: The Br is on carbon 2, but the class is not the locant. The carbon carrying Br is bonded to three other carbons (two CH₃ groups and a CH₂CH₃ group), so 2-bromo-2-methylbutane is tertiary.
In 3-bromopentane the carbon carrying the Br atom is bonded to two other carbon atoms (two CH₂ groups), so the compound is a secondary halogenoalkane.

Two Br atoms do not make a halogenoalkane secondary. The class depends on the carbon carrying the halogen, and here that carbon is bonded to only one other carbon atom, so the compound is not secondary.
The class counts carbon atoms, not hydrogen atoms, on the carbon carrying the halogen. That CH₂ carbon is bonded to one other carbon, so 1-bromopentane is primary.
questions.explain: In 3-bromopentane the carbon carrying the Br atom is bonded to two other carbon atoms (two CH₂ groups), so the compound is a secondary halogenoalkane.

questions.q: The diagram shows four skeletal formulas, P, Q, R and S. Which one represents a structural isomer of butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃?
options: compound P
compound S
compound Q
compound R
optionWhy: P is butan-2-ol itself, drawn with the chain running the other way: OH on the third carbon from the left is OH on carbon 2 when numbered from the right. A different drawing is not a different compound.
S is 2-methylpropan-1-ol, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH, molecular formula C₄H₁₀O, the same as butan-2-ol but with a branched chain: a structural isomer.
Q is but-3-en-2-ol, C₄H₈O. It has four carbon atoms and one oxygen, but two fewer hydrogen atoms than C₄H₁₀O, so its molecular formula differs and it is not an isomer.
R is pentan-2-ol, C₅H₁₂O, the next member of the same homologous series as butan-2-ol. Isomers must have the same molecular formula.
questions.explain: S is 2-methylpropan-1-ol, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂OH, molecular formula C₄H₁₀O, the same as butan-2-ol but with a branched chain: a structural isomer.

questions.q: Which compound can exist as cis and trans isomers?
options: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene
1,3-dichloropropane
2-bromo-3-methylbutane
1,2-dimethylcyclobutane
optionWhy: A C=C bond is necessary but not sufficient. Each carbon of this C=C carries two identical CH₃ groups, so swapping sides gives the same molecule.
This is an open chain with only single C–C bonds. Free rotation lets the chlorine atoms take any relative position, so there are no cis and trans isomers.
Carbon 2 of this molecule is chiral, so it has a pair of enantiomers. That is optical isomerism, not cis–trans isomerism, which needs a C=C bond or a ring.
The ring restricts rotation, and carbons 1 and 2 each carry two different groups (a CH₃ group and an H atom). The two CH₃ groups can be on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans) of the ring.
questions.explain: The ring restricts rotation, and carbons 1 and 2 each carry two different groups (a CH₃ group and an H atom). The two CH₃ groups can be on the same side (cis) or opposite sides (trans) of the ring.

questions.q: Which compound has a chiral carbon atom?
options: propan-2-ol
butan-2-ol
but-2-ene
chloroethane
optionWhy: Carbon 2 carries the –OH group, but its other groups are H and two identical CH₃ groups. A chiral carbon needs four different groups.
Carbon 2 of butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, is bonded to four different groups: H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃. The molecule is therefore chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers.
But-2-ene shows cis–trans isomerism, a different kind of stereoisomerism. None of its carbon atoms is bonded to four different groups.
The molecule has different ends, but no carbon atom carries four different groups (each has at least two H atoms), so it is not chiral.
questions.explain: Carbon 2 of butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, is bonded to four different groups: H, OH, CH₃ and CH₂CH₃. The molecule is therefore chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers.

questions.q: The diagram shows two skeletal formulas, P and Q, of pent-2-ene. Which statement about P and Q is correct?
options: P and Q are the same compound, since the chain can rotate freely about the C=C bond.
P and Q are cis–trans isomers, since rotation about the C=C bond is restricted.
P and Q are enantiomers, since each is the non-superimposable mirror image of the other.
P and Q are structural isomers, since the chain is drawn bent in different directions.
optionWhy: Rotation about a C=C bond would require the π bond to break, so it does not occur at ordinary temperatures. The two arrangements cannot interconvert and are different compounds.

The π bond prevents rotation about C=C, and each double-bond carbon carries two different groups (H and CH₃; H and C₂H₅). In P the CH₃ and C₂H₅ groups are on the same side (cis); in Q on opposite sides (trans).
Neither molecule has a chiral carbon atom, and Q is not the mirror image of P: the two differ in whether the groups are on the same or opposite sides of the C=C. They are cis–trans isomers.
Both have the same connectivity, CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH₃, so they are not structural isomers. The difference is a fixed spatial arrangement about the C=C bond, which makes them stereoisomers.
questions.explain: The π bond prevents rotation about C=C, and each double-bond carbon carries two different groups (H and CH₃; H and C₂H₅). In P the CH₃ and C₂H₅ groups are on the same side (cis); in Q on opposite sides (trans).

questions.q: The diagram shows stereochemical formulas of two halogenoalkanes, P and Q. Which statement is correct?
options: Both are chiral, since each has a carbon atom bonded to Cl, H and two alkyl groups.
Both are chiral, since the mirror image of each, with Cl and H swapped, looks different.
Neither is chiral, since neither has a C=C bond to restrict rotation.
Only P is chiral, since its central carbon atom carries four different groups.
optionWhy: A carbon atom is chiral only if all four groups differ. In Q the two alkyl groups are both CH₃, so the mirror image of Q is superimposable on Q and Q is not chiral.

A mirror-image drawing that looks different is not necessarily a different molecule. Q's mirror image can be turned over to superimpose exactly on Q, because two of its groups are the same (CH₃). Only a carbon atom bonded to four different groups, as in P, gives a non-superimposable mirror image.
Restricted rotation about C=C gives cis–trans isomerism, a different kind of stereoisomerism. Chirality arises from a carbon atom bonded to four different groups, which P has.

In P the central carbon is bonded to H, Cl, CH₃ and C₂H₅, four different groups, so it is a chiral centre and P exists as a pair of enantiomers. In Q two of the groups are CH₃, so its mirror image is superimposable.
questions.explain: In P the central carbon is bonded to H, Cl, CH₃ and C₂H₅, four different groups, so it is a chiral centre and P exists as a pair of enantiomers. In Q two of the groups are CH₃, so its mirror image is superimposable.

questions.q: The mass spectrum of pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃ (M_r = 86), has a molecular ion peak at m/z 86 and a peak at m/z 57. Fragment data: m/z 29 = C₂H₅⁺ or CHO⁺; m/z 57 = C₄H₉⁺ or C₂H₅CO⁺. Which species is responsible for the peak at m/z 57?
options: the ion C₂H₅CO⁺, left when C₂H₅ (mass 29) is lost from the molecular ion
the ion C₂H₅⁺, left behind when a fragment of mass 57 is lost
an impurity of M_r 57 in the sample, as pure pentan-3-one gives only M⁺
the ion C₄H₉⁺, since the data table lists m/z 57 as C₄H₉⁺
optionWhy: Breaking the bond between the carbonyl carbon and one ethyl group gives C₂H₅CO⁺ (m/z 57) and an uncharged C₂H₅ fragment of mass 29 (86 − 57 = 29). Only the charged fragment is detected.
The m/z value of a peak is the mass of the detected ion, not the mass lost. A peak at m/z 57 is an ion of mass 57; the piece lost has mass 86 − 57 = 29.
Peaks below the molecular ion are fragment ions from pentan-3-one itself. The peak at m/z 57 is C₂H₅CO⁺, formed when C₂H₅ (mass 29) is lost from M⁺ (86 − 57 = 29).
m/z 57 can be C₄H₉⁺ or C₂H₅CO⁺. Pentan-3-one has no unit of four carbons without the oxygen, so C₄H₉⁺ cannot form by breaking one bond; the ion is C₂H₅CO⁺.
questions.explain: Breaking the bond between the carbonyl carbon and one ethyl group gives C₂H₅CO⁺ (m/z 57) and an uncharged C₂H₅ fragment of mass 29 (86 − 57 = 29). Only the charged fragment is detected.
questions.working: Mass lost from M⁺ = 86 − 57 = 29, which corresponds to C₂H₅ (2 × 12 + 5 × 1 = 29). Detected ion: C₂H₅CO⁺ = 2 × 12 + 5 × 1 + 12 + 16 = 57. The alternative C₄H₉⁺ (4 × 12 + 9 = 57) would need four carbon atoms bonded together without the oxygen, which pentan-3-one does not contain.

questions.q: A compound, C₃H₆O₂, has an IR spectrum with a very broad absorption across 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ and a strong absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹. Characteristic ranges: O–H (alcohols) 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; O–H (carboxylic acids) 2500–3000 cm⁻¹; C–H 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; C=O 1700–1750 cm⁻¹; C=C 1620–1680 cm⁻¹. Which interpretation is correct?
options: It is an alcohol: the broad band is the O–H of a hydroxyl group.
It is an ester: the 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ band is due only to C–H bonds.
It is a carboxylic acid: there is a broad acid O–H band and a C=O band.
It has a C=C bond, which causes the absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹.
optionWhy: Alcohol O–H absorbs at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹. A very broad band at 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ is the O–H of a carboxylic acid.
C–H absorptions are sharper and lie at 2850–3090 cm⁻¹. A very broad band spreading down to 2500 cm⁻¹ is the hydrogen-bonded O–H of a carboxylic acid.
A very broad band across 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ is the O–H of a carboxylic acid, and 1715 cm⁻¹ lies in the C=O range, 1700–1750 cm⁻¹. The compound is propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH.
C=C absorbs at 1620–1680 cm⁻¹. An absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹ is in the C=O range, 1700–1750 cm⁻¹.
questions.explain: A very broad band across 2500–3000 cm⁻¹ is the O–H of a carboxylic acid, and 1715 cm⁻¹ lies in the C=O range, 1700–1750 cm⁻¹. The compound is propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH.

questions.q: The diagram shows the IR spectrum of a compound with molecular formula C₄H₈O₂. Characteristic ranges: O–H (alcohols) 3200–3600 cm⁻¹, broad; O–H (carboxylic acids) 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, very broad; C–H 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; C=O 1700–1750 cm⁻¹; C=C 1620–1680 cm⁻¹; C–O 1050–1410 cm⁻¹. To which class does the compound belong?
options: an ester, as the band at 1740 cm⁻¹ is C=O and there is no O–H band
a carboxylic acid, as the band at 2850–3000 cm⁻¹ is the carboxyl O–H
an unsaturated compound, as the band at 1740 cm⁻¹ is a C=C absorption
an ether, as the strong band at 1240 cm⁻¹ shows a C–O bond
optionWhy: The very strong, narrow band at 1740 cm⁻¹ is C=O, and the strong bands near 1240 and 1050 cm⁻¹ are C–O. Nothing appears at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and the absorption at 2850–3000 cm⁻¹ is narrow (C–H), not the very broad acid O–H, so the compound is an ester, such as ethyl ethanoate.
The band near 2980 cm⁻¹ is narrow, as C–H absorptions are. The O–H of a carboxylic acid is very broad, spreading across 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, and no such band is present.
C=C absorbs at 1620–1680 cm⁻¹ and is usually weak. A very strong band at 1740 cm⁻¹ lies in the C=O range, 1700–1750 cm⁻¹.
A C–O band is present in ethers and esters alike, but an ether has no C=O bond. The very strong band at 1740 cm⁻¹ shows a C=O group, so the compound is an ester, not an ether.
questions.explain: The very strong, narrow band at 1740 cm⁻¹ is C=O, and the strong bands near 1240 and 1050 cm⁻¹ are C–O. Nothing appears at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and the absorption at 2850–3000 cm⁻¹ is narrow (C–H), not the very broad acid O–H, so the compound is an ester, such as ethyl ethanoate.
questions.working: The band at 1740 cm⁻¹ lies in the C=O range, 1700–1750 cm⁻¹. The narrow band near 2980 cm⁻¹ lies in the C–H range, 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; there is no band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹ and no very broad band across 2500–3000 cm⁻¹, so there is no O–H. Bands at 1240 and 1050 cm⁻¹ lie in the C–O range, 1050–1410 cm⁻¹. C=O plus C–O with no O–H: an ester.

figure.alt: IR spectrum: transmittance / % (0 to 100, upwards) against wavenumber / cm⁻¹ from 4000 on the left to 500 on the right. The line stays near 95% from 4000 to about 3050, shows a narrow, medium dip near 2980, returns to 95%, then a very strong narrow dip near 1740, a medium dip near 1370, a strong dip near 1240, a medium dip near 1050 and a small dip near 940. There is no absorption between 3100 and 4000. The axis is numbered 4000, 3000, 2000, 1500, 1000 and 500.

questions.q: A compound, C₂H₄O₂, is either ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, or methyl methanoate, HCOOCH₃. Its ¹H NMR spectrum shows two singlets, at δ 2.1 and δ 11.5. Typical chemical shifts: R–COOH 9.0–13.0 ppm; H on a carbon bonded to the singly bonded O of an ester, –C(=O)–O–CH₃, 3.7–4.8 ppm. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Methyl methanoate: its two H environments give two singlets.
Methyl methanoate: an O–H proton gives no signal, so the acid gives one.
Ethanoic acid: δ 11.5 is the CH₃ group, as it has the most H atoms.
Ethanoic acid: δ 11.5 is the COOH proton and δ 2.1 is the CH₃ group.
optionWhy: Methyl methanoate would also give two singlets, so the number and splitting of signals cannot decide. Its CH₃O signal would be in the 3.7–4.8 ppm range; δ 11.5 points to a COOH proton.
The O–H proton of a carboxylic acid does give a signal, in the range 9.0–13.0 ppm. Ethanoic acid therefore gives two signals, matching the spectrum.
The compound is right but the assignment is not. Chemical shift depends on the environment, not the number of H atoms; the number of H atoms shows in the area. δ 11.5 is the COOH proton.
A signal at δ 11.5 lies in the range for R–COOH, 9.0–13.0 ppm, and methyl methanoate has no hydrogen in that range. The CH₃ group of ethanoic acid gives the singlet at δ 2.1.
questions.explain: A signal at δ 11.5 lies in the range for R–COOH, 9.0–13.0 ppm, and methyl methanoate has no hydrogen in that range. The CH₃ group of ethanoic acid gives the singlet at δ 2.1.

questions.q: The diagram shows the high-resolution ¹H NMR spectrum of chloroethane, CH₃CH₂Cl. Which statement about the splitting is correct?
options: The signal at δ 3.6 is the CH₃ group, because three H atoms give 3 + 1 = 4 lines.
The signal at δ 3.6 is a quartet because the adjacent CH₃ group carries three H atoms.
The signal at δ 1.5 is the CH₂ group, as its carbon has two other atoms bonded to it.
The signal at δ 3.6 shows an environment containing four equivalent H atoms.
optionWhy: n counts hydrogen atoms on the neighbouring carbon, not in the group itself. The CH₃ group is next to CH₂ (n = 2) and gives the triplet at δ 1.5; the quartet is the CH₂ group.
The CH₂Cl hydrogens are deshielded by chlorine and appear at δ 3.6. Their only neighbouring carbon is the CH₃ group, with n = 3 hydrogen atoms, so the signal is split into n + 1 = 4 lines.
Splitting is not caused by the atoms bonded to the carbon but by hydrogen atoms on adjacent carbons. The CH₂ group is next to CH₃ (n = 3), so it is the quartet, at δ 3.6.
The number of lines shows the number of neighbouring hydrogen atoms plus one, not the size of the group. Chloroethane has no group of four equivalent hydrogen atoms; the quartet is CH₂ split by CH₃.
questions.explain: The CH₂Cl hydrogens are deshielded by chlorine and appear at δ 3.6. Their only neighbouring carbon is the CH₃ group, with n = 3 hydrogen atoms, so the signal is split into n + 1 = 4 lines.
questions.working: CH₂Cl hydrogens: the neighbouring CH₃ carbon carries n = 3 H atoms, so the signal has n + 1 = 4 lines (quartet). CH₃ hydrogens: the neighbouring CH₂ carbon carries n = 2, so 2 + 1 = 3 lines (triplet).

One signal centred at about δ 3.6 consists of four closely spaced lines, the inner two taller than the outer two. A second, taller signal centred at about δ 1.5 consists of three closely spaced lines, the middle one tallest.

questions.q: Compound Y, C₄H₈O (M_r = 72), gives these data. IR: a strong absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹, sharp absorptions at 2850–3000 cm⁻¹ and no absorption between 3100 and 3700 cm⁻¹ (ranges: C=O 1700–1750 cm⁻¹; C–H 2850–3090 cm⁻¹; O–H in alcohols 3200–3600 cm⁻¹; C=C 1620–1680 cm⁻¹). MS: M⁺ at m/z 72, peaks at m/z 57 and m/z 43. ¹H NMR: δ 1.0 (triplet, 3H), δ 2.1 (singlet, 3H), δ 2.4 (quartet, 2H). Which structure is consistent with all the data?
options: Butanal, CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO: the strong band at 1715 cm⁻¹ with no O–H band identifies the aldehyde C=O group.
2-Methylpropanal, (CH₃)₂CHCHO: its three hydrogen environments give the three signals observed.
Butanone, CH₃COCH₂CH₃: the δ 2.1 singlet is CH₃CO and the ethyl group gives the triplet and quartet.
But-3-en-1-ol, CH₂=CHCH₂CH₂OH: the strong absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹ is due to its C=C bond.
optionWhy: The IR band fits an aldehyde as well as a ketone, but the ¹H NMR spectrum does not: butanal has four hydrogen environments (CHO, CH₂, CH₂, CH₃) and no 3H singlet, whereas the spectrum has three signals including a singlet.
The number of signals is right, but the areas and splitting are not. Its two equivalent CH₃ groups would give a 6H doublet and the CH and CHO signals 1H each, not areas of 3:3:2 with a 3H singlet.

The C=O band with no O–H fits a ketone or aldehyde. Three signals of areas 3:3:2 with a singlet, a triplet and a quartet fit CH₃CO–CH₂CH₃: the CH₃ next to C=O has no neighbouring H (singlet), and the ethyl group gives a triplet and quartet. Loss of CH₃ (15) gives m/z 57 and loss of C₂H₅ (29) gives m/z 43.
C=C absorbs at 1620–1680 cm⁻¹; 1715 cm⁻¹ is in the C=O range. An alcohol would also give a broad O–H band at 3200–3600 cm⁻¹, and none is present.
questions.explain: The C=O band with no O–H fits a ketone or aldehyde. Three signals of areas 3:3:2 with a singlet, a triplet and a quartet fit CH₃CO–CH₂CH₃: the CH₃ next to C=O has no neighbouring H (singlet), and the ethyl group gives a triplet and quartet. Loss of CH₃ (15) gives m/z 57 and loss of C₂H₅ (29) gives m/z 43.
questions.working: M_r = 4 × 12 + 8 × 1 + 16 = 72, matching M⁺ at m/z 72. Loss of CH₃ (15) gives 72 − 15 = 57, the C₂H₅CO⁺ ion; loss of C₂H₅ (29) gives 72 − 29 = 43, the CH₃CO⁺ ion. Signal areas 3 + 3 + 2 = 8 hydrogen atoms, matching C₄H₈O.
